title: Panzanella
subtitle: Tuscan bread and tomato salad with red onion and capers
excerpt: Panzanella is a Tuscan summer salad made with stale bread soaked in water, squeezed out, and mixed with ripe tomatoes, red onion, capers, and basil in a red wine vinegar and olive oil dressing. The bread softens and absorbs the dressing without falling apart.
sourceNotes: Panzanella is a Tuscan peasant dish with roots in the practice of using up stale bread rather than wasting it. It is mentioned in 16th-century Italian poetry and has been a Tuscan summer staple for centuries. The dish varies between Florentine (with soaked bread torn in chunks) and Sienese (bread rubbed dry) versions. The modern Florentine version, with soaked and squeezed bread, is the most widely made today.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble the salad up to 30 minutes before serving. Do not dress it more than 30 minutes ahead or the bread will become too soft.

content.text: Panzanella is stale bread, ripe tomatoes, red onion, capers, and basil, dressed with red wine vinegar and olive oil. The bread is soaked in cold water and squeezed out before it goes into the salad, which sounds strange but gives it a soft, absorbent texture that drinks up the dressing. It is a summer dish made in 20 minutes from what is left at the end of the week. Like all Italian bread dishes, it depends on the quality of the olive oil and the ripeness of the tomatoes.

items.prepNote: stale, torn into 3 to 4 cm chunks

content.text: Place the bread chunks in a bowl and cover with cold water. Leave for 5 minutes until saturated. Lift the bread out in handfuls and squeeze firmly to remove as much water as possible. It should be damp but not dripping. Place in a large serving bowl.
Season the tomatoes with salt and leave for 5 minutes. Add them to the bread along with all their juice.
Add the red onion, capers, and torn basil. Drizzle over the red wine vinegar and olive oil. Toss gently to combine.
Leave to sit for 20 to 30 minutes before serving. Taste and adjust salt and vinegar. The salad is best at room temperature, not cold.

Panzanella is Tuscan, from the tradition of cucina povera (poor kitchen) that turned stale bread into a meal with whatever was to hand. It is mentioned in 16th-century Italian poetry and has barely changed since. The controversy in Italy is whether the bread should be soaked and squeezed (the Florentine method) or rubbed dry (the Sienese method). Both produce a good salad; this recipe uses the Florentine approach.
